chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub al-Kazzaz, from Yazid al-Kunasī, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the divorce of a pregnant woman, so he said: 'He divorces her with one divorce for the waiting period of months, with witnesses.' I said: 'And is it permissible for him to take her back?' He said: 'Yes, and she is his wife.' I said: 'If he took her back and consummated the marriage, then he wanted to divorce her with another divorce?' He said: 'He does not divorce her until a month passes for her after he has consummated the marriage.' I said: 'If he divorced her a second time and witnessed, then took her back and witnessed upon her return, and consummated the marriage, then divorced her with the third divorce and witnessed upon her divorce—for each waiting period a month—does she become completely divorced from him as the woman who is divorced three times becomes, so that she is not permissible to her husband until she marries another husband?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'What is her waiting period?' He said: 'Her waiting period is that she gives birth to what is in her belly, then she is permissible to the husbands.'

key_terms.تَضَعُ مَا فِي بَطْنِهَا: She gives birth to what is in her belly

ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period (iddah) for a pregnant woman in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinct 'iddah (waiting period) of a pregnant woman, which is determined by the duration of pregnancy rather than menstrual cycles. It further elucidates the procedural nuances of revocation and finality in divorce, confirming that upon childbirth, she becomes fully eligible for remarriage to others, a ruling foundational to Shia family law.
